modules.name: Clock
modules.header:
Reading a clock, and waiting on one.
`ClockMonotonic` counts forward from an arbitrary point and never jumps; `ClockRealtime` tracks wall time and can
move in either direction. A duration is measured with the first, a timestamp taken from the second.
FreeBSD numbers its clocks differently from Linux — monotonic is 4 here and 1 there — which is why an identifier
must never be carried between the two packages.

modules.name: Dynamic
modules.header:
Loading a shared object at run time, and finding a symbol inside it.
The one part of the FreeBSD interface that is not a system call: resolution, relocation and reference counting all
belong to the run-time linker, whose entry points live in libc.

modules.name: Entropy
modules.header:
Unpredictable bytes, from the kernel's own generator.
The only source in this package fit for a key, a token, or anything an adversary would like to guess. FreeBSD's
generator is always seeded by the time user code runs, so unlike Linux's there is no first-boot wait to think
about — but a short count is still possible and still has to be looped over.

modules.name: Errors
modules.header:
How a FreeBSD system call reports failure, and the numbers it reports.
FreeBSD does not report an error the way Linux does. The kernel sets the carry flag and leaves a *positive* errno
in the result register, so the raw instruction result cannot be tested for sign. The assembly wrappers in
`Syscall` normalize that to Linux's convention — a small negative number — so everything above them reads the
same on both systems, and `IsError` and `Errno` are then the same two functions.
The names keep the system's own spelling, because `EINVAL` is what a man page names. The values below are
FreeBSD's, which agree with Linux for the first thirty-four and then diverge.

modules.name: File
modules.header:
Reading and writing through a file descriptor, and the three descriptors a process starts with.
Each wrapper returns the normalized raw result: a byte count, or a small negative error number. A short count is
not an error and not an end of file — only a zero-length read means the source has ended.
The three descriptor constants are annotated `int32` rather than `FileDescriptor`, because a `const` cannot name a
type alias declared in another file of the package.

modules.name: Memory
modules.header:
Mapping and unmapping address space, and moving the program break.
Nothing here tracks what it hands out: an address from `Mmap` is valid until `Munmap` releases exactly the range
that was mapped.

modules.name: Poll
modules.header:
Waiting on many descriptors at once, and descriptors that never wait: `kqueue(2)` and the `O_NONBLOCK` flag.
A kqueue is itself a descriptor. A `Kevent` both registers interest, as a change, and reports readiness, as an
event; reading and writing are separate filters, so a descriptor wanted for both is registered twice. The
registrations here are level-triggered: a descriptor is reported for as long as it is ready.

modules.name: Process
modules.header:
What a process can ask or say about itself.
Nothing here creates a process: a raw binding to `fork` and `execve` without signal handling, descriptor
inheritance and a wait protocol would be an invitation to get all three wrong.

modules.name: Resolve
modules.header:
Finding the addresses of a host by name, which is the C library's work rather than the kernel's: it reads the
hosts file, asks the name servers the system is configured with, and follows whatever else the system's name
service switch says. That is why this module links a library, and why a program that resolves names is linked
dynamically.

modules.name: Socket
modules.header:
Sockets: endpoints of network connections and datagrams, reached through the system calls that make and use them.
Addresses are passed as the `sockaddr` bytes the kernel reads, built by the caller, so these wrappers stay as thin
as the rest of the package. Name resolution is not a system call and lives in `Rux/Net`.

modules.name: Spawn
modules.header:
Starting another program, waiting for it, and stopping it.
A new process is started with the C library's `posix_spawnp`, which runs the setup a child needs between its creation
and the start of the new program — duplicating descriptors, opening files, changing directory — from a list of
actions the parent builds, and reports a failure to start as an error number rather than a child that exits. That
is why this module links a library, and why a program that starts processes is linked dynamically.

modules.name: Syscall
modules.header:
The raw system-call entry points, and the numbers that select a call.
Every wrapper elsewhere in this package is one of these seven functions with the arguments named. A caller may use
them directly for a call this package does not wrap, which is what they are public for.
Unlike Linux, both supported architectures share one numbering: FreeBSD assigns a call its number once, in
`syscalls.master`, and every architecture uses it. What differs is only where the number and the arguments go.
A raw result from these wrappers is already normalized to Linux's convention — a value, or a small negative error
number — which is what `Errors::IsError` and `Errors::Errno` read.

modules.name: Thread
modules.header:
Threads of execution, which the C library manages: their stacks, their thread-local blocks and joining them.
The kernel only starts and stops a thread; everything a program needs around that belongs to the C library, and a
thread started behind its back would have no thread-local block. That is why this module links a library, and why
a program that starts threads is linked dynamically.
The names are the platform's own, lowercase, because they are the symbols the library exports and what a reader
porting code will look for.

modules.name: Types
modules.header:
The kernel ABI's own types: what a FreeBSD system call takes and gives back.
FreeBSD's 64-bit ABI fixes each width, so these are the same on both supported architectures and none of the
`long` questions that `Rux/C` has to answer arise here.

modules.name: Umtx
modules.header:
Waiting on a word in memory until another thread changes it, which is what every lock is built on.
`_umtx_op(2)` puts the calling thread to sleep only if the word still holds the value the caller last saw, and
checks that in the kernel, so a wake that lands between the caller's check and its sleep is never lost. Only the
private forms are bound: the word is never shared with another process.

items.name: Nanosleep
items.signature: pub func Nanosleep(request: *Timespec, remaining: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
doc.markdown:
Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
`remaining` is written when a signal cut the wait short, and may be null. Returns zero, or a negative error
number; `EINTR` with the unslept time in `remaining` is how a signal is reported.
`request` must be non-null, and its nanoseconds must be under one second.

params.name: remaining
params.markdown: receives the unslept time when a signal cut the wait short, and may be null

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_FAST`: like `ClockMonotonic`, read from a cached value rather than the hardware.
doc.markdown:
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC_FAST`: like `ClockMonotonic`, read from a cached value rather than the hardware.
Cheaper and coarser. FreeBSD offers this pairing where Linux offers a coarse clock under a different number.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_REALTIME_FAST`: like `ClockRealtime`, read from a cached value.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_REALTIME_FAST`: like `ClockRealtime`, read from a cached value.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this process has used.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID`: processor time this process has used.

Returns zero, or a negative error number. The resolution is the granularity the clock advances by, not the cost

`resolution` must be non-null and writable.

doc.markdown: `RTLD_LAZY`: resolve a function symbol the first time it is called rather than at load.

doc.summary: `RTLD_NOW`: resolve every symbol before `dlopen` returns.

doc.markdown: `RTLD_GLOBAL`: make this object's symbols available to objects loaded afterwards.

items.name: dlopen
items.signature: pub extern func dlopen(filename: *char8, flags: int32) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Loads a shared object and returns a handle to it, or null on failure.
doc.markdown:
Loads a shared object and returns a handle to it, or null on failure.
A name without a slash is resolved by the loader's own search rules, and one with a slash as a path. A second
call for an object already loaded returns the same handle and raises its reference count rather than loading
it twice. Failure is reported through `dlerror`, not errno.

params.name: filename
params.markdown: a NUL-terminated name or path, or null for the main program

params.name: flags
params.markdown: `RTLD_LAZY` or `RTLD_NOW`, combined with the other `RTLD_*` flags

doc.returns: a handle for `dlsym` and `dlclose`, or null with the reason in `dlerror`

items.name: dlsym
items.signature: pub extern func dlsym(handle: *var opaque, symbol: *char8) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Finds a symbol in a loaded object and returns its address, or null.
doc.markdown:
Finds a symbol in a loaded object and returns its address, or null.
A null return is ambiguous, since a symbol whose address is legitimately zero exists. Clear `dlerror` by calling
it, then call this, then read `dlerror` again to tell the two apart.
doc.returns: the symbol's address, or null

items.name: dlclose
items.signature: pub extern func dlclose(handle: *var opaque) -> int32

doc.summary: Drops one reference to a loaded object, unloading it when the last one goes.
doc.markdown:
Drops one reference to a loaded object, unloading it when the last one goes.
Every address obtained from the object through `dlsym` becomes invalid once it is actually unloaded, which this
gives no way to observe.
doc.returns: zero on success, and non-zero with the reason in `dlerror`

doc.summary: Reports the most recent loader error and clears it, or returns null when there is none.
doc.markdown:
Reports the most recent loader error and clears it, or returns null when there is none.
The message points at storage the loader owns and a later call may reuse. Reading it clears the error, so two
calls in a row report the second as no error at all.
doc.returns: a NUL-terminated message, or null

doc.summary: `GRND_NONBLOCK`: report rather than wait.
doc.markdown: `GRND_NONBLOCK`: report rather than wait. Present for parity; FreeBSD's generator does not block.

doc.summary: `GRND_RANDOM`: accepted and ignored, which is what FreeBSD does with it.
doc.markdown: `GRND_RANDOM`: accepted and ignored, which is what FreeBSD does with it.

items.name: GetRandom
items.signature: pub func GetRandom(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint, flags: uint32) -> int64

doc.summary: Fills up to `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills up to `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
Returns the number of bytes actually written, or a negative error number. A request over 256 bytes may be cut
short, and a caller needing the whole buffer must call again for the rest.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. Treat a short count as bytes obtained, not as failure, or the
unwritten tail stays whatever it held — which for a key is the worst possible outcome.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes to ask for

params.name: flags
params.markdown: zero, or one of the `Random*` values

doc.returns: the bytes written, which may be fewer than asked for, or a negative error number

items.name: Read
items.signature: pub func Read(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *var opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
doc.markdown:
Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
`buffer` is borrowed and written. Returns the number of bytes read, zero at end of file, or a negative error
number. A short count is ordinary.
`buffer` must be writable for `count` bytes.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to ask for

doc.returns: the bytes read, zero at end of file, or a negative error number

doc.markdown:
Writes up to `count` bytes from `buffer` to `fd`.
`buffer` is borrowed and read. Returns the number of bytes written, or a negative error number. A short count is
ordinary and the rest has to be written by calling again.
`buffer` must be readable for `count` bytes.
doc.returns: the bytes written, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
doc.markdown:
Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. A failure does not mean the descriptor is still open, so retrying a
failed close can close one another thread has since opened under the same number.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
`directoryFd` is `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path. `mode` is read only when `OpenCreate` is set.
`path` must be non-null and terminated. The mode is masked by the process umask.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.markdown: the path to open, as a null-terminated byte string

params.markdown: the access mode and the open flags, combined with `|`

params.markdown: the permission bits for a file this creates, ignored otherwise

doc.returns: the new descriptor, or a negative error number

doc.markdown:

The buffer holds packed `dirent` records: the file number at offset 0 (8 bytes), a seek cookie at 8 (8 bytes),
the record's length at 16 (2 bytes), the entry type at 18 (1 byte), padding at 19, the name's length at 20
(2 bytes), padding at 22, and the name from 24. The kernel writes as many whole records as fit.
The fourth parameter is named as macOS names `Getdirentries64`'s, which is the same output.
